To the Honorable Justices of the United States
Supreme Court:1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Louisiana District Attorneys Association
(“LDAA”) is a Louisiana non-profit corporation which
includes as its members all of the District Attorneys
and assistant district attorneys in the State of
Louisiana.2 The LDAA is controlled by a 17 -member
Board of Directors composed of elected district
attorneys and appointed assistant district attorneys.
The petitioner’s requested relief could have far -
reaching impact on the justice system in the State of
Louisiana. The LDAA Board of Directors reviewed the
above-captioned matter and authorized the instant
filing.
The Mission of the LDAA focuses on the
improvement of the Louisiana Criminal Justice
System. A cornerstone of that system is the
framework for criminal jury trials. Louisiana allows
trial by a six -person jury for numerous offenses. The
current structure has been established and utilized

2

for more than 60 years prior to the grant of certiorari
in the instant matter. Granting the requested relief
would have substantial negative impact on the justice
system in the State of Louisiana. That impact would
be borne primarily by Louisiana’s District Attorneys.
The amicus cur iae is presented to this
Honorable Court for consideration to support the
Respondent and to highlight the substantial negative
impact on the State of Louisiana. This is clearly
within the mission statement of this Organization.
Based on the above -described representations, the
LDAA respectfully asserts that it has the requisite
interest for the instant filing.

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Louisiana’s current constitution requires  a
graduated system of jury size  for criminal settings ,
utilizing six-person juries. La. Const. art. I, §17; see
also La. C.Cr.P. art. 782. The graduated structure
expedites trial and creates efficiency in the system .
There is no indication that Louisiana’s legal
framework produces unreliable convictions  when
utilizing six -person juries . The fundamental role of
the jury to prevent governmental overreach is
preserved.  An overruling of the Williams decision
would ignore significant historical perspectives and
create substantial burden on the State of Louisiana.
Williams v. Florida , 399 U.S. 78, 90 S.Ct. 1893, 26
L.Ed.2d 446.

3

ARGUMENT
I. Louisiana’s Current Legal Framework
Under the Louisiana Constitution, there are
four separate categories of criminal trials: capital,
absolute felonies, relative felonies, and bench trials.
Id. Undergirding this structure is the Louisiana Code
of Criminal Procedure's basic taxonomy of offenses: a
“felony” is any offense that might be punished by
death or by imprisonment at hard labor, while a
“misdemeanor” is any other offense.  La. C.Cr.P. art.
933(3) and (4); compare with Fl. Stat. 775.08 (defining
a felony as any offense with a potential punishment of
imprisonment over one year).
Capital cases involve those where a sentence of
death may be imposed. The 12-person jury is used in
a bifurcated process , with separate phases for guilt
and sentencing.  La. Const. art. I, § 17; see also La.
C.Cr.P. art. 905 .2. The jury in a capital case
determines guilt and the appropriate sentence . Our
constitution prevents the joinder of capital matters
with non- capital felonies. Absolute felon ies carry a
sentence that must be imposed with hard labor. They
are tried before a jury of twelve. State v. Breaux, 24-
737, (La. 5/9/25); 408 So.3d 899, 903. A relative felony
carries a sentence that may either be imposed at hard
labor or without hard labor . Id. The proviso “at hard
labor” refers to the authority under which the
incarceration is served. At hard labor sentences are
served under the authority Louisiana Department of
Public Safety and Corrections  (DPS&C), rather than
under the authority of a local sheriff. See generally,
La. R.S. 15:824; see also State v. Lisenby, 534 So. 2d

4

996, 997 (La. Ct. App. 1988) . This designation does
not, alone, require a judge to impose a term of
incarceration. La. C.Cr.P. art. 893.
Duncan misdemeanors are non-felony offenses
which have sentences that are greater than 6 months
but that cannot be imposed at hard labor. La. C.Cr.P.
art. 779, see also: Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U.S. 145,
88 S. Ct. 1444, 20 L. Ed. 2d 491 (1968). This
encompasses a wide variety of crimes—from
prohibitions on taking albino alligators (La. R.S.
56:280), to cyberstalking (La. R.S. 14:40.3), to
graverobbing (La. R.S. 8:653). Duncan and its
progeny indicate that the language of the constitution
(“all crimes” and “all criminal prosecutions”) confers
the jury trial right only to serious offenses . Ballew v.
Georgia, 435 U.S. 223, 245, 98 S. Ct. 1029, 1041, 55 L.
Ed. 2d 234 (1978); and Burch v. Louisian a, 441 U.S.
130, 136, 99 S. Ct. 1623, 1627, 60 L. Ed. 2d 96 (1979).
Through this line of cases, this Court has assured the
states that waived juries, guilty pleas, and bench
trials for petty offenses were not impacted.
Homicide provides a clear example of how the
graduated structure of offense and modes of trial is
applied in Louisiana.  Capital murder req uires a
twelve-person jury  to determine both guilt and the
appropriate sentence (life vs. death) . La. R.S. 14:30 .
Second-degree murder carries a mandatory life
sentence at hard labor and the 12- person jury
determines only the guilt of the accused. Sudden heat
of passion killings fall under manslaughter, another
absolute felony carrying a potential 40-year sentence.
A killing through  criminal negligence is a relative
felony punishable by up to 15 years  and would be
reviewed by a six-person jury. La. R.S. 14:32. A killing

5

through reckless operation  of a watercraft  is a
Duncan misdemeanor and is tried before the smaller
jury option . La. R.S. 34:851.6.   Our legislature has
separated out numerous “levels” of homicide based on
the decreasing culpability of the accused.  This
balances efficiency with the heightened scrutiny
preferred where severe sentences are more common.
In addition to graduated penalties, the mode of
trial also correlates with the imposition of sentence.
An offender convicted of an absolute felony  must be
sentenced to hard labor and  be housed under the
custody of the DPS&C. Judges retain discretion over
the sentences in relative felonies and misdemeanors.
They retain control on how the felony sentence is
imposed; either with hard labor or without hard labor.
This discretion maximizes the ability of the judge to
craft a narrowly tailored  sentence for each unique
criminal defendant . The judge also has greater
discretion to reduce or suspend those sentences.  La.
C.Cr.P. art. 881.  The relative felony can also receive
greater consideration for alternatives to jail , like
home incarceration  or commitment to a community
rehabilitation facility . La. C.Cr.P. art. 894.2  & La.
R.S. 15:1133. Imprisonment under the custody of the
local sheriff has traditionally allowed greater access
to trustee status and provides fewer barriers to
participation in work release programs.  La. R.S.
15:711, see also La. R.S. 15:708.
The six-person jury has never been Louisiana's
default rule for all offenses. The graduated system
allows for the balance of efficiency with the protection
against state over -reach guaranteed by the Sixth
Amendment. A trial before a six -person jury for
simple drug possession could be accomplished in a

6

single day . Conversely, voir dire to select a death -
penalty qualified jury panel could, alone, take weeks.
A defendant facing the possibility of death is not
similarly situated to a defendant facing six months
and a day. Weeks-long voir dire on every routine drug
possession case would be completely untenable.
Louisiana’s system accounts for these realities.
II. Louisiana, Jurisprudence, and History
Louisiana’s structure has functioned well for
more than a century . Louisiana’s criminal justice
system has substantial roots in this reliable and
efficient structure for criminal trials.
Any historical review of the jury trials in the
English common law must also acknowledge the
governmental structure and the likely criminal
sanction involved with those proceedings . From the
medieval period forward, death was described as the
“sanction for all English felonies, including minor
instances of larceny.”  Robert L. Jones, Finishing a
Friendly Argument: The Jury and the Historical
Origins of Diversity Jurisdiction , 82 N.Y.U. L. Rev.
997, 1026 (2007). The death penalty was so ubiquitous
that the English capital code of the eighteenth century
was nicknamed the “Bloody Code” and “subjected a
vast and increasing number of property crimes to the
death penalty.” Peter King & Richard Ward,
Rethinking the Bloody Code in Eighteenth -Century
Britain: Capital Punishment at the Centre and on the
Periphery, 228 Past & Present 159 (2015). The
prevalence of a 12- person jury makes sense in this
context: all felons met the same end and deserved the
same protection. The current system reserves capital
punishment for the most severe of offenders.

7

Historically, juries themselves  were far
different from those in our current system. They were
at liberty to ignore the judge and the law . Jones,
Finishing a Friendly Argument at 1026. The courts in
England at the time of the founding were answerable
to the Crown and the jury was a method of preserving
local autonomy. Id. at 1027. Corruption of common law
jurors may have occurred regularly, and jurors would
acquit for reasons completely unrelated to the facts or
law (e.g. “reputation of the accused” or disagreement
on the severity of the offender’s  particular rape).
Thomas Andrew Green, Verdict According to
Conscience: Perspectives on the English Criminal
Trial Jury, 1200–1800, at 26 (1985). The Constitution
balanced the potential vices of the juries, the severity
of criminal punishments, and the power of the
judiciary.
Interestingly, the right of a jury trial in English
common law was predicated on the consent of the
accused. C onsent had a definition at the time that
“somewhat different than our own.” Singer v. United
States, 380 U.S. 24, 27, 85 S. Ct. 783, 786, 13 L. Ed.
2d 630 (1965). This Court acknowledged that the peine
forte et dure  existed at the same time our Founders
were confronting the impending Revolution. Id. That
practice tortured non-consenting criminal defendants
until they died or consented to a jury trial. Id. The
practice was only abolished in 1772.  Id. The
replacement deemed those who stood mute in a
criminal proceeding and failed to consent to a jury  to
have pleaded guilty . Id. This was the English law
effective at the time our Constitution was enshrined.
These practices would have been as synonymous with
the word “jury” as the composition of 12 persons.

8

Against that backdrop , the development of
Louisiana’s law  surrounding juries  is logical. The
Louisiana Territory was purchased little more than a
decade after the ratification of the Constitution.
Shortly thereafter, the territorial legislature
endeavored to incorporate English common law . La.
Acts of 1805, C. 50 §33; see also J. Denson Smith, The
Louisiana Criminal Code: Its Background and
General Plan, 5 La. L. Rev. 1 (1942). The 1805 “Crimes
Act” gave wholesale adoption of English legal
tradition. Id. Ironic, considering that the Act  was
simultaneously published in French.  This was a
system of law “about which at that time the people of
Louisiana knew and could know practically nothing
about.” Id. at 2. The results were problematic. It was
eloquently described that “the Louisiana lawyer was
forced to resort to the confusing precedents and obtuse
distinctions of the English c ommon law.” Dale E.
Bennett, Louisiana Criminal Procedure —A Critical
Appraisal, 14 La. L. Rev. 1 (1953).  The disfavor of a
wholesale adoption of other systems of law was
quickly expressed in the Louisiana Constitution of
1812, after statehood was achieved . There, the
adoption of laws or legal systems by general reference
was overtly prohibited. La. Const. of 1812, art. IV § 11
This provision survives 214 years later in our current
state constitution. La. Const. art. III, § 15. A grant of
relief in the instant matter would require exactly that:
a State with a strong civilian history would be forced
into adoption of a system of laws through the
historical divinations of a federal judge.
The distinctions between the U.S.
Constitution, Louisiana’s history, and the English
common law at the time of the founding can be seen

9

in other areas. As noted on pages 9- 10 of the
respondents brief in opposition of certiorari, the
“vicinage” requirement for jury trials existed at the
time of the founding in English common law. Some
Framers advocated for its inclusion in the Bill of
Rights, but it was not adopted into the  Sixth
Amendment. Contrast that to Louisiana’s first two
constitutions which guaranteed “a speedy public trial
by an impartial jury of the vicinage.”  La. Const. of
1812, art. VI, § 18; La. Const. of 1845, art. VI,  § 107.
The state constitution diverged from its federal
counterpart until 1864, where the “district” language
was adopted . La. Const. of 1864, art. VII § 105.
Customs gave way to clarity and vicinage gave way to
district.
The first reference to a specific number of
jurors appeared in Louisiana’s Constitution  of 1879.
La. Const. of 1879, art. VII. The importance of a local
jury was emphasized and authority over a jury’s size
was expressly granted to the Legislature. This was
contained in the same constitution which insisted
that “[n]o qualification of any kind for suffrage or
office, nor any restraint upon the same, on account of
race, color, or previous condition shall be made by
law.” La. Const.  of 1879, art. 188.  In the same
constitution that outlawed racial discrimination for
voting and office, the jury size was addressed. As with
vicinage, we see a potential remnant of English
Common law shed in favor of the graduated
framework of jury sizes that continues until today.
The need for this change was summarized well
in State v. White . There, the court analyzed the
changes in mode of trial that occurred between state
constitutions. State v. White, 33 La. Ann. 1218, 1220

10

(1881). Earlier constitutions organized parish courts
which convened monthly. Id. The 1879 Constitution
abolished the parochial courts and mandated  two
regular jury terms a year for district courts. This was
balanced by authorizing trial for lesser offenses by a
five-person jury. Succinctly stated: “[t]he object which
they [the legislature] had in view is very apparent; it
was to secure the chances of a speedy trial to the
accused and to relieve the parishes of the enormous
expense and great inconvenience of drawing,
summoning, and empaneling large numbers of jurors
five or six times a year.”  Id. Ironically, that court
grappled with a similar argument made by the
petitioner: that the origins of common law juries
prohibited Louisiana’s approach. In response, the
court stated “[w]e cannot agree with counsel for the
accused in their patriotic alarm fo r the safety of the
principles of Magna Charta [sic] under such a
construction, or that such a doctrine is repugnant to
common law traditions or jurisprudence.”  Id. A trial
before the smaller jury could be conducted in a shorter
time and at a lower cost, while still affording the
accused sufficient protection from state overreach.
The 1898 Constitution further codified this
practice. La. Const. of 1898, art. 116.  After its
adoption, Louisiana courts consistently interpreted
this provision as a  non-waivable jurisdiction
limitation. State v. Reeves, 128 La. 37, 39, 54 So. 415,
415 (1911).  Legislative authority over the juror
qualifications was clearly established by Louisiana’s
state supreme court. State v. Jones, 8 Rob. (LA) 573,
582 (1845).  This was extended over the number of
persons that qualified as a valid jury.  State v.
Gutierrez, 15 La. Ann. 190, 192 (1860).  The Reeves

11

analysis remained in effect until 2006, when it was reexamined in Louisiana. State v. Jones, 2005-0226 (La.
2/22/06), 922 So. 2d 508. In this latter Jones matter
(2006), heavy reliance was placed on the  Williams
holding to conclude that an impermissibly larger jury
was a harmless error . Id. at 510- 12. Petitioner now
urges this Court to overturn  Williams. Absent that
reliance, r elative felonies in Louisiana may  become
un-prosecutable. The state constitution would place a
jurisdiction limit on presenting a relative felony to a
12-person jury and petitioner’s requested relief would
prevent the use of anything else.
The development of the jury size occurred as
the Legislature’s organization of the courts
progressed in the State. This slow progression is a far
cry from the historical perspective that the petitioner
urges this Court to accept: that the smaller jury
sprang to life in the heads of newly unencumbered
racists at the end of Reconstruction. The consistent
effort toward a more efficient justice system is the
cornerstone of this procedure. The conclusion that a
twelve-person jury was an “accidental feature” of the
Sixth Amendment was adopted and enshrined in
Louisiana jurisprudence.

III. Detrimental Impact
The petitioner’s requested relief would
negatively impact the administration of Louisiana’s
criminal justice system. The District Attorneys of
Louisiana urge that the  State’s reliance interest in
preserving these convictions is strong . The
jurisdictional crisis that such relief creates, as
discussed above, would require substantial legislation
and a constitutional amendment to remedy. Beyond

12

that, burden placed upon local courts could be
overwhelming.
There are over 400 relative felony offenses in
Louisianan’s legal framework. This encompasses
nearly every conceivable designation of offense from
vehicular homicides (impaired driving homicide, La.
R.S. 14:32.1) , provisions of our criminal hazing  law
(La. R.S. 14:40.8 ) and many Louisiana felony -level
drug possession statutes  (La. R.S. 40:967(C),
40:968(C), and 40:969(C) ). Louisiana law embraces
the graduated system of offenses described in section
one of the instant filing. The need for efficiency in the
system is paramount.
At the time of the instant filing, official La.
DPS&C data reflects an inmate population of 31,412.
3 This represents those that have been convicted of a
felony and who received a sentence at hard labor
within Louisiana.  Nearly half of that population,
some 15,273 inmates , are currently serving a
sentence for a relative felony . For 7,106 of those
inmates, a relative felony is their longest sentence of
conviction. This does not include those who receive a
sentence for a relative felony that is not at hard labor
or those who are incarcerated on a Duncan
misdemeanor.
There is no readily available method to identify
which of those convictions were the result of a jury
trial. Similarly, there is no readily available method
to determine which of these cases are currently
pending on direct appeal. This number would increase
when accounting for cases with sentences that are

3 Demographic information was provided by the Executive
Counsel for La. DPS&C and the Departments’ publicly available
“Demographic Dashboard” website.

13

“without hard labor,” Duncan misdemeanors, and
those that the trial court placed on a suspended
sentence (i.e. probation). The potential impact of the
petitioner’s requested relief could upset thousands of
convictions in Louisiana.
Petitioner’s requested relief  would create
unintended consequences . The instant matter
involves a felony. Petitioner’s requested relief is not
attached to the level of offense, but rather the mode of
trial. The overruling of Williams would not inherently
alter the opinion in Duncan. In Louisiana, this would
extend the impact of petitioner’s requested relief to
more than 300 additional offenses.

IV. Conclusion
The negative impact of petitioner’s requested
relief on Louisiana would be significant. Our State
would immediately inherit an unknown number of
cases for re-trial. Substantial portions of our statutory
structure would require revision. A constitutional
crisis would be foisted upon our state courts to
resolve. Hundreds to thousands of convictions would
be upset.  If that number was sufficiently high,
prosecutors may be forced to triage their caseloads ,
rather than seek justice in each matter.
A broad decision in this matter would give
chilling corporeality to the specter of additional jury -
related claims. The Ramos definition adopted a
common law preference for unanimity.  Ramos v.
Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 140 S.Ct. 1390, 206 L.Ed.2d
583. Relief in this matter would mandate  a common
law fixation on 12- person juries. The future of jury
trial waivers, guilty pleas, and other rights that have
become essential to our system would seem suddenly

14

unsettled. Most states define what qualifies as a
juror. Many people who serve on modern juries would
have been unjustly denied participation at the time of
the founding: women, people of color, nonlandowners, convicted felons, etc . Incorporating a
250-year-old definition of jury size, without also
incorporating the companion definitions of a “juror” is
inconsistent.
The Sixth Amendment guarantees a trial
before a jury. The Amendment does not provide a
number for a group to become a jury and that appears
intentional. The only descriptive word assigned to the
jury was impartial. Contrast that with the adjectives
attached to the trial itself: speedy and public. The use
of a six-person jury greatly reduces the cost and time
of a jury trial. This is uncontrovertibly true. As
argued, the District Attorneys of Louisiana believe
that the six -person jury is a reliable and thorough
protection for the accused. The relief sought would
have this Court act as editors of the Constitution,
rather than interpreters. It asks that you insert a
number that does not exist and bold a section that
bears no such emphasis. Creating a uniform
requirement for a 12-person jury would be done at the
cost of the Framer’s  actual emphasis: the right of an
accused to quickly dispose of the controversy.
Assuming arguendo that this court finds for the
petitioner, application should be prospective only.
Retroactive application thwarts the intent of the
criminal justice system, undermines the solemnity of
juror participation, retraumatizes victims, and places
an insurmountable burden on a state whose resources
are stretched nearly threadbare. The administration
of justice requires a level of  certainty, and as the

15

Court noted in Edwards v. Vannoy , quoting Teague,
“constitutional rules not in existence at the time a
conviction became final seriously undermines the
principle of finality which is essential to the operation
of our criminal justice system.”  Edwards v. Vannoy,
593 U.S. 255, , 141 S. Ct. 1547, 1554, 209 L. Ed. 2d
651 (2021). In this matter , retroactive application of
any new procedural rule would force the state’s hand
in retrying thousands of cases . The Court further
noted that it has repeatedly  held that new rules of
criminal procedure do not a pply retroactively on
federal collateral review. Depiction of the watershed
rule as “moribund” should be sufficient.  Id. at 272.
The prosecutors of Louisiana faced the tidal wave of
collateral relief claims related to Ramos and the
likelihood of the same impact here is high, should this
Court grant petitioner’s relief . As Edwards followed
Ramos, so too would Kian likely beckon additional
cases to seek this Court’s review.
 The Constitution guarantees a trial , which
petitioner received . It guarantees a jury, which
petitioner received. The guarantees of due process, as
imposed on the States through the Fourteenth
Amendment, have been satisfied.  The petitioner was
advised of the charges against him and presumably
represented by counsel at all critical stages. There
was no compulsion to incriminate himself  and there
is no indication in the pleadings that he was denied
compulsory process. Petitioner’s path to the jury was
vastly different that that of the 18 th-century English
defendant. With the protections provided on that
path, State of Florida proved his accusations beyond
a reasonable doubt. Petitioner ’s injury, if any exists ,
is that a greater swath of the public was not forced to

16

surrender their time to assess his flagrant and
criminal conduct. The argument makes no real effort
to even assert that a greater jury size would have
garnered a different result in this case. The six-person
jury that unanimously found this offender guilty
provided a sufficient safeguard against a “corrupt or
overzealous prosecutor and against the compliant,
biased, or eccentric judge.” Duncan, 391 U.S. at 156.
The protections of the Constitution were satisfied.

Amici respectfully prays that the petitioner’s
relief be denied.

Respectfully submitted,
